issues.issue: The covenant is conditioned on "concurrent legislation ... having the same effect as this Part", but nothing defines when legislation has the "same effect"; the phrase is a boilerplate recital of mutual assent rather than an operative term.
The doubled period in "Short title.." is a typographical slip that changes nothing about meaning.

"Area of drainage into the Delaware River and its tributaries, including Delaware Bay" leaves the landward boundary of the basin to hydrology rather than a described line, but the term is workable in practice.

"Compact" is defined as Part I only, yet the enacted instrument also contains Part II reservations (Section 15.1) that operate on the same subject matter, so the reach of the defined term is not self-evident.
"Net induced adverse effects, whether or not compensated for" is an open-ended component of "cost" with no measuring convention, and "indirect expenditures" has no stated boundary.

The definition of "facility" piles specific enumerations onto the catch-all "or to facilitate any other uses of any of them" and "any and all things and appurtenances necessary, useful or convenient", leaving the reach of the general words against the specifics genuinely uncertain.
"Facility" is a building block of the "project" definition in Section 1.2(g), which in turn drives the Section 3.8 approval requirement, so its breadth is contested through those provisions.
"Any appropriate branch, department, bureau or division thereof, as the case may be" leaves which federal component is "appropriate" undetermined.

"Project" is defined by a sprawling sentence whose modifiers are ambiguous: it is unclear whether "separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission" qualifies all of the listed works, and whether "for the conservation, utilization, control, development or management of water resources" limits the whole definition or only the "separate facility" branch.

Read with Section 3.8, which subjects to Commission approval any "project having a substantial effect on the water resources of the basin", the definition either swallows private activity generally or is confined to Commission-identified works, and the two provisions cannot both be given their natural reading.

"Signatory party" includes the federal government, yet many operative sections speak instead of "signatory states" (e.g., Sections 1.6(a), 3.4), so which body a duty falls on varies with the label used.

"Water resources" is defined to include "related natural resources" and "related uses of land" without saying what makes a resource or land use "related", so the definition's outer edge is indeterminate.

The finding that "a single administrative agency is therefore essential" sits against Section 1.5, which preserves existing offices and agencies, and Sections 11.1(c) and 11.2(c), which keep federal, state and local agency authority intact.

The declaration that the basin's waters are "ample to meet all presently projected demands" points the other way from the operative shortage machinery in Sections 10.2 to 10.4, which assume protected areas and water supply emergencies.

"Equal and uniform treatment to all water users who are similarly situated" is a purpose statement with no stated test for similar situation, and it is the sort of declared purpose parties invoke to color operative powers.

Section 15.1(t) makes the United States' membership contingent on this section surviving constitutional challenge, and Section 15.1(q) reserves Congress's unilateral right to amend, which sits uneasily with the all-party amendment rule of Section 14.20.
"To the fullest extent it finds feasible and advantageous" makes the Commission the judge of its own directive, so the mandatory "authorized and directed" language has no measurable content.

The renewal window "not later than 20 years nor sooner than 25 years prior to the termination" inverts the usual order of the limits and reads on its face as an impossible condition until the reader reverses it.
Winding up is left to "such manner as may be provided by act of the Congress", with no default if Congress never acts and no role for the states that may have triggered termination.

Section 15.1(d) of Part II provides that the President's member and alternate "shall serve at the pleasure of the President", which contradicts this section's "to serve during the term of office of the President"; the compact's own endnote acknowledges the two were inconsistent.
The alternate's tenure "during the term of the member appointing him" is overridden for the federal alternate by Section 15.1(d), which puts him at the President's pleasure.
"Shall serve without compensation" is contradicted for the federal member by Section 15.1(r), which permits the President to fix compensation paid by the United States notwithstanding Section 2.4.

"A majority of the membership" does not say whether the quorum measure is the full five-member body or those present, and Section 14.5(a) shows the drafters knew how to say "full membership" when they meant it.

"Necessary or convenient to effectuate its powers or duties within the basin" is an elastic test for acting outside the basin, and the consent sentence does not say whether consent is needed for the sale of water outside the basin as well.

The water resources program described here must cover "such reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine", while Section 13.2 fixes "the ensuing six years" as the default; the two descriptions of the same instrument do not line up exactly.

"In accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment" imports an undefined body of judicial doctrine as the standard governing allocations, and the extent to which it constrains the Commission is not stated.

The paragraph uses "unanimous consent" twice for different bodies — the parties to the decree and the Commission's own members — so which unanimity governs an emergency change is not immediately clear.

The statement that no allocation "shall be deemed to constitute an apportionment of the waters of the basin" is hard to square with the chapeau of Section 3.3, which directs the Commission to allocate "in accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment".

"Any proper party deeming itself aggrieved" is undefined, and the section splits review between Supreme Court original jurisdiction and "any court of competent jurisdiction" without saying which actions fall on which side.

The waiver is qualified by two exceptions of uncertain reach — proceedings "to effectuate rights, powers, duties and obligations under Section 3.3" and those "required to effectuate" specified decree paragraphs — so how much of the right to seek modification survives is contestable.

The blanket protection of the decree is expressly subject to Sections 3.3 and 3.4, which themselves authorize emergency alterations of decree diversions, so the boundary between protection and permitted interference must be worked out across the three sections.

Subparagraph (h) adds a catch-all — "such other and different powers" and "all powers necessary or convenient to carry out its express powers or which may be reasonably implied therefrom" — on top of seven enumerated powers, leaving the reach of the general words against the specifics genuinely open.

The rate-setting power "without regulation or control by any signatory party" is cut back by Section 15.1(b), which bars charges for withdrawals or diversions that could lawfully have been made free on the effective date, and by Section 3.5(b).

The trigger "project having a substantial effect on the water resources of the basin" turns on two undefined and contestable expressions — the defined-but-circular term "project" and the vague qualifier "substantial effect" — with no threshold given for either.

Whether this approval requirement reaches private activity at all depends on the definition of "project" in Section 1.2(g), which ties projects to works "separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission"; the two provisions pull in opposite directions on the Commission's jurisdiction.

"To this end, but with limitation thereto, the commission may" is a mechanical error: every parallel provision (Sections 3.5, 4.1, 3.6(b)) says "without limitation thereto", and as written the phrase converts an illustrative list into an exhaustive one.

The broad power to construct and operate water supply facilities is limited by Section 4.5, which forbids the Commission to "engage in the business of distributing water", and the line between the two is not drawn.
The list of storage-and-release purposes closes with "and other purposes", an unbounded catch-all appended to an enumerated list.

The prohibition is framed negatively — a signatory party must not "permit any augmentation of flow to be diminished by the diversion of any water" — without saying what degree of diminution counts or how a party is to police diversions it has already authorized.

Assessments may be levied on users "specially benefited thereby to a measurable extent" but must not "exceed the actual benefit", two benefit measures that are stated without any method of computation.

"Engage in the business of distributing water" is undefined and sits directly against the granted power to "provide storage, treatment, pumping and transmission facilities", so where transmission ends and distribution begins is open.

The control standard — that pollution "shall not injuriously affect waters of the basin as contemplated by the comprehensive plan" — uses an undefined injury threshold and makes the plan, rather than the compact, the measure.

The covenant is measured by aspirational adjectives — "satisfactory condition", "after reasonable treatment", "free from unsightly or malodorous nuisances" — that supply no enforceable standard, and it closes with the catch-all "such other uses as may be provided by the comprehensive plan".

The Commission's enforcement power over dischargers coexists with Section 5.5, which preserves each signatory party's own pollution authority, and with Section 15.1(k), which preserves federal officers' water-pollution functions.

The preservation of each state's power to impose "additional conditions and restrictions" on pollution is hard to reconcile with Section 10.8, which supersedes conflicting state permits, and with the Commission's assumption of pollution jurisdiction under Section 5.2.

The standards are called "recommended", yet Section 6.3 requires the Commission's flood-lands acquisitions to be "in accord with the standards adopted and promulgated pursuant to Section 6.2", leaving unclear whether they are advisory or binding.

The power to "establish encroachment lines" and to set "standards for flood plain use" reads as regulatory, while Section 6.2(a) describes the same instrument as "recommended standards" that do not restrict local zoning.
"Unwarranted constrictions that reduce the ability of the river channel to carry flood water" supplies no benchmark for what makes a constriction unwarranted.

The bar on operation until the Commission finds "no other suitable unit or agency of government is available to operate the same upon reasonable conditions" leaves both "suitable" and "reasonable conditions" to the Commission's own judgment with no stated criteria.

The mandatory duty to "provide for the development" of recreational facilities is made "subject to" Section 8.2(b), which forbids the Commission to operate any such facility when another agency is available.

The bar on operation until the Commission finds "no other suitable unit or agency of government is available to operate the same upon reasonable conditions" leaves "suitable" and "reasonable conditions" undefined.

The mandatory sealed competitive bidding for concessions is displaced by Section 15.1(l), which provides that Section 8.4 "shall not be construed to apply to facilities operated pursuant to any other Federal law".

Impoundment for power "in accordance with the comprehensive plan" must be read with Section 3.5, which bars interference with the New Jersey v. New York decree, and with Section 1.4's reservation of Congress's navigable-waters powers.

"Wholesale marketing of power" is set against a prohibition on "the business of direct sale to consumers" without defining either, and "where such facilities are not otherwise available upon reasonable terms" adds a second undefined condition.
"Reasonable, nondiscriminatory, and just" states three overlapping rate standards with no ratemaking methodology or reference point.

The power to delegate regulation to signatory parties runs against Section 10.8, which supersedes conflicting state permits, and against New York's Section 637, which conditions acceptance of any delegation on independent state power.

Protected areas may be declared where demands "have developed or threaten to develop to such a degree as to create a water shortage", a wholly predictive standard with no threshold, and "water shortage" is itself undefined.

The grandfathering of permits "heretofore granted under the laws of any of the signatory states" is difficult to square with Section 10.8, which provides that state-issued diversion or withdrawal permits are superseded to the extent of any conflict with Commission regulation.
"A drought or other condition which may cause an actual and immediate shortage" combines a general catch-all with the single specific of drought and a purely anticipatory trigger.

The permit standard turns on avoiding depletion that "will adversely affect ... the just and equitable interests and rights of other lawful users", a phrase that supplies no rule for ranking competing uses beyond "due regard".

Judicial review is provided for determinations under Sections 10.2 to 10.5 but the section is silent on emergency declarations under Section 10.4's first sentence, inviting an expressio unius argument about what is reviewable.

The supersession of state permits "to the extent of any conflict" cannot easily be reconciled with Section 10.3(ii), which excepts previously granted state permits, or with Section 5.5's and Section 1.5's preservation of state authority.
"All projects related to powers delegated to the commission" leaves the relatedness test undefined, so which federal projects require consultation is not fixed.

The sentence has no stated subject — "No expenditure or commitment shall be made ... nor shall it be deemed authorized" — leaving both who is barred and what "it" refers to to be supplied by inference.

The absolute bar on unplanned federal expenditure conflicts with Section 11.1(c), which preserves each federal agency's existing authority to construct and operate projects, and with Section 15.1(s), which subordinates the plan to federal powers.

Preserving each federal agency's authority "except as specifically provided by this section" is in tension with Section 11.1(b), which bars any expenditure on a project not first included in the comprehensive plan.
"All projects related to powers delegated to the commission" gives no test for relatedness, leaving the scope of the state consultation duty open.

The bar on state and local expenditure for projects not in the comprehensive plan sits against Section 11.2(c), which preserves state and local agency authority, and against Section 3.8, which uses a different trigger ("substantial effect") for Commission approval.

Preserving state and local authority "except as specifically provided by this section" is hard to reconcile with Section 11.2(b)'s absolute bar on expenditure for projects not in the comprehensive plan.

The reserved state right to levy charges measured by withdrawals runs against Section 3.5(b), which forbids fees on decree-permitted diversions, and Section 3.7, which puts Commission charges beyond signatory-party control.
"Equitable cost sharing and reimbursement formulas" is a mandate without a standard, and the four enumerated items are introduced by "including" so their relation to the general duty is open.

The signatory parties' pledge of technical and administrative services is expressly cut down for the United States by Section 15.1(h), which limits the federal pledge to what agencies agree to or the President directs.

Bonds are said to be "payable solely out of the properties and revenues of the commission without recourse to taxation" and in the same breath to be "direct and general obligations" backed by the Commission's "full faith and credit", two characterisations that pull against each other.

The sentence declares that "the purpose of this compact shall include ... all costs of any project", apparently a drafting slip for the purposes for which bonds may be issued; read literally it expands the compact's purposes rather than the permitted uses of bond proceeds.
The bar on pledging any signatory party's credit sits against Section 12.20(b), which allows bonds to be sold "with or without the guaranty of such signatory party".

The indenture may contain any covenants "other than any restriction on the regulatory powers vested in the commission by this compact", but the boundary between a permitted rate covenant and a forbidden restriction on regulatory power is not drawn.
"No bond or its terms shall mature in more than fifty years from its own date" is oddly phrased — terms do not mature — but the fifty-year limit is otherwise definite.

The unqualified exemption "from all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties" is limited as to the United States by Section 15.1(f), which preserves federal internal revenue taxation of the bonds.
The amended rule that bonds bear interest "at a rate determined by the commission" sits against Section 12.13, which still caps net interest cost at six percent per annum on bonds sold below par.

The section opens with unfettered discretion to "fix terms and conditions for the sale or other disposition" of bonds and then imposes mandatory sealed-bid, advertisement and net-interest-cost rules, so how far the opening grant is qualified by what follows is contestable.

The mandatory public sale on sealed proposals is displaced by Section 12.20(b), which permits delivery of bonds to a signatory agency "without public offering" notwithstanding any other provision of the compact.
A judgment in an in rem validation proceeding is declared "conclusive against all persons whomsoever", a sweeping preclusion whose reach against absent parties is not spelled out.

The revenues are declared a trust fund that "shall not be used or pledged for any other purpose" except as the indenture provides for "expenses for other purposes including administration, operation, maintenance, improvements or extensions of the facilities or other purposes", an exception whose closing catch-all can swallow the rule.

The section enumerates two bondholder remedies and then says the enumeration "does not, however, exclude ... any other rights or remedies", leaving the reach of the general saving language against the specifics open.

The signatory parties "will provide such capital funds required" and then the same sentence disclaims "any mandatory obligation", so the promise is arguably illusory and its residual content must be construed.

Permitting bonds to be sold "with or without the guaranty of such signatory party" is difficult to square with Section 12.3, which denies the Commission any power to pledge the credit of a signatory party.

The plan "shall include all public and private projects and facilities which are required, in the judgment of the commission", a mandatory-sounding duty whose content is left entirely to the Commission's own judgment and to the contested term "projects".

Inclusion in the comprehensive plan is the operative trigger for Sections 11.1(b) and 11.2(b), yet Section 3.8 uses a different trigger ("substantial effect on the water resources of the basin") for the same subject matter.

The six-year program period stated here differs from Section 3.2(b), which describes the same water resources program by reference only to "such reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine".

The residual balance is to be "apportioned equitably among the signatory parties" with no formula, and the apportionment requires a unanimous vote that the section does not say how to break if it fails.

The parties "covenant and agree" to include the apportioned amounts in their budgets but the promise is made "subject to such review and approval as may be required by their respective budgetary processes", which arguably makes the covenant unenforceable.

"Enter intro contracts" is an evident typographical error for "into", and subparagraph 6's "all corporate powers essential to the declared objects and purposes" adds an unbounded catch-all to the enumerated powers.
The public-hearing and filing requirements are excused for a rule "which deals solely with the internal management of the commission", a category with no definition and an obvious boundary problem.

An investigator or watchman is "vested with the powers of a peace officer of the state in which he is duly assigned", importing four different bodies of state law without saying which powers transfer.

The in-lieu payment obligation applies "as to specific projects" and is measured by "the taxes lawfully assessed upon property for the tax year next prior to its acquisition ... for a period of ten years", a formula whose ten-year period and per-project scope are both ambiguously placed in the sentence.

The section fixes ten days' posted notice for hearings "in all other cases wherein this compact requires a public hearing", which must be squared with the differently worded notice requirements elsewhere, such as Section 3.7 and Section 10.2's "public hearing upon due notice".

Removal of the executive director requires "a majority of the full membership", a different measure from Section 2.5's "majority of the membership", and the contrast invites argument about what Section 2.5 requires.

Appointments must be "solely on the basis of merit and fitness" with no "residence test", yet the sanction attaches only to an officer or employee "found by the commission to be guilty of a violation" — the commissioners who make the appointments are not covered.
"Financially interested, either directly or indirectly, in any contract" has no de minimis or attribution rule, so what counts as an indirect interest is left entirely open.

The forfeiture sanction reaches only an "officer or employee", although Section 14.8(a) imposes the prohibitions on "commissioner, officer or employee"; the omission of commissioners invites an expressio unius reading that they face no forfeiture.
"Knowingly made" does not say whose knowledge voids the contract — the Commission's, the officer's, or the counterparty's — which decides whether an innocent contractor loses its bargain.

"Lowest responsible bidder" is undefined, and the five enumerated waiver grounds include the open-textured "the public exigency requires the immediate delivery" and "services ... of a specialized or professional nature".

Subjecting the Commission's financial transactions to General Accounting Office audit is in tension with Section 15.1(m), which provides that for the listed federal purposes "the commission shall not be considered a Federal agency".
"Refuse to give all require assistance" is a grammatical error for "all required assistance", though the sense is recoverable.

The exception "other than property of a signatory party and any property held ... in connection with a diversion authorized by a United States Supreme Court decree" is grammatically ambiguous as to whether both categories are excluded from the eminent domain power or only the first.

The Commission's share of relocation cost "shall not in any event exceed the expenditure required to serve the public convenience and necessity", a cap stated in a phrase that supplies no measure of the required expenditure.
The blanket right of way is "subject to such reasonable conditions as the highway department of the signatory party may require", leaving the reasonableness of conditions to be settled case by case.

The penalty clause is syntactically garbled — "a penalty of not less than $50 nor more than $1,000 for each such offense to be fixed by the court which the commission may recover" — leaving the relative clause attached to "court" rather than to the penalty.

Measuring the Commission's tort responsibility by the law applicable to United States officers cannot easily be squared with Section 15.1(m), which provides that the Commission "shall not be considered a Federal agency" for purposes of the Federal Tort Claims Act provisions there listed.

The disclaimer that nothing affects state riparian-rights law is hard to reconcile with Section 14.14(a), which expressly empowers the Commission to condemn riparian rights, and with the allocation power in Section 3.3 and the permit regime in Article 10.

Requiring amendments to be concurred in by all signatory parties conflicts with Section 1.4 and Section 15.1(q), which reserve to Congress the unilateral right to revise, amend or repeal the terms on which the United States remains a party.

The direction that the compact "be reasonably and liberally construed" states two potentially competing interpretive commands and is itself the kind of instruction parties invoke to widen or narrow other provisions.

The thirty-day delay for effectiveness sits against the Part II effectuation sections of Delaware, New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania, each of which provides that "this act shall take effect immediately".
